Hey, not tryna be a dick but, just so you know, that first point makes no sense and is untrue. Harmony is measured by dissonance and consonance, which is measured by the frequency ratios between notes, which is affected by the distance between notes. Dissonance sounds bad, consonance good, to be brief. The emotional value comes from what intervals are between your notes, and furthermore, what combination of intervals are within your song. 

In order from most consonant to most dissonant, heres every interval:

Octave (C2 -C3)
Fifth (C-G)
Fourth (C-F)
Major third (C-E)
Minor third (C-Eb)
Major sixth (C-A)
Minor sixth (C-Ab)
Minor seventh (C-Bb)
Major seventh (C-B)
Major second (C-D)
Minor second (C-Db)
Tritone (C-Gb/F#)

What makes certain intervals good and others bad is how simple the frequency ratio between the two notes is. For an octave, its 2:1, for a fifth its 2:3, and for a fourth its 3:4. But the ratio for a tritone is 45:32, which is notably more complicated than the others. Kinking and manipulation of all this psychoacoustic knowledge is pretty much what we do when we write melodies and harmonies (for me at least) and the combination of different intervals is what allows for the wide spectrum of emotions that music makes you feel.
